title: Rabbi Yehudah ben Beteira (בתירא—בתירה) (I)
author: Aharon Hyman

paragraphs: Rabbi Yehudah ben Beteira (בתירא—בתירה) (I). Hyman writes that he still saw the Temple standing, like all his colleagues, Rabbi Eliezer, Rabbi Yehoshua, Rabbi Akiva and Rabbi Tarfon. In Temple times his great academy was in Nisibis, as in [Sanhedrin 32b](https://www.sefaria.org/Sanhedrin.32b.10), where they said, “Follow Rabbi Yehudah ben Beteira to Nisibis.” [Pesachim 3b](https://www.sefaria.org/Pesachim.3b.10-12) relates that a certain Aramean used to go up and eat Passover offerings in Jerusalem (deceiving them that he was a Jew). He came to Rabbi Yehudah ben Beteira and said to him:

“It is written, ‘No foreigner shall eat of it,’ and here I eat of the choicest of the choice.” (Hyman asks: What did Rabbi Yehudah ben Beteira understand, that he could catch him in a snare? For with the Passover offering ‘the choicest of the choice’ does not apply.) He said to him: “Did they feed you from the fat tail?” He said to him, “No.” He said to him: “When you go up there, tell them: Feed me from the fat tail.” When he went up, he said to them, “Feed me from the fat tail.” They said to him: “The fat tail goes up to the altar.” When they asked who had told him to ask for it, he answered, “Rabbi Yehudah ben Beteira.”

They investigated his background, found that he was an Aramean, and killed him. They sent to Rabbi Yehudah ben Beteira: “Peace be with you, Rabbi Yehudah ben Beteira, for you are in Nisibis and your net is spread in Jerusalem.” Hyman concludes: From this we see clearly that he lived in Temple times; and he sees further proof in [Mikvaot](https://www.sefaria.org/Mishnah_Mikvaot.4.5) (4:7 in his citation)[^10], where Rabbi Yehudah ben Beteira said, “An incident with the trough of Yehu that was in Jerusalem,” etc. He also saw the destruction of the Temple, as in [Pesachim 109a](https://www.sefaria.org/Pesachim.109a.5): “It was taught: Rabbi Yehudah ben Beteira says: When

the Temple stood, there was no rejoicing except with meat … and now that the Temple does not stand, there is no rejoicing except with wine.” Of Rabbi Yehudah ben Beteira’s family we find in [Sanhedrin 92b](https://www.sefaria.org/Sanhedrin.92b.4): “Rabbi Yehudah ben Beteira stood on his feet and said: I am of their descendants (of the dead whom Ezekiel revived), and these are tefillin that my paternal grandfather left me from them.” (Although in the Gemara his words are arranged after Rabbi Yehudah and Rabbi Eliezer, the son

of Rabbi Yose HaGelili, Hyman thinks that his words there refer to the words of Rabbi Yehoshua and Rabbi Eliezer.) As for his ancestors, Hyman considers it very likely that they were of the Benei Beteira, who stepped down from their patriarchate and handed it to Hillel, and one of them went down to Nisibis and founded a great academy there, and Rabbi Yehudah ben Beteira is of their descendants. Their sons are mentioned as being in the days of Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai, as in [Rosh Hashanah 29b](https://www.sefaria.org/Rosh_Hashanah.29b.12-13), where Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai said to the Benei Beteira, “Let us blow.”

Hyman writes: We do not find anywhere who his teachers were; he explains this by saying that he undoubtedly received [his Torah] from his father in Nisibis. Afterward, when all the sages of the generation settled in Yavneh, his voice was heard among them (for every one of the chief sages of that generation had an academy of his own in his place of residence, as in [Sanhedrin 32b:10](https://www.sefaria.org/Sanhedrin.32b.10), but they would come periodically to the great assembly house in Yavneh to clarify the halakhah), as in Negaim 9:3 and 11:7, where they asked

Rabbi Eliezer, and he said, “I have not heard.” Rabbi Yehudah ben Beteira said to him, “May I reason it out?” Rabbi Eliezer said to him: “You are a great sage, for you have upheld the words of the sages.” In Eduyot 8:3: “Rabbi Yehoshua and Rabbi Yehudah ben Beteira testified … Rabban Gamliel said: We have accepted your testimony,” etc.; and in Pesachim 3:3 he disagrees with Rabbi Yehoshua; in Peah 3:7 he disagrees with Rabbi Tarfon, and the halakhah follows his words; in Kelim 2:4 he disagrees with Rabbi Akiva; and in [Shabbat 96b:20](https://www.sefaria.org/Shabbat.96b.20) he said to Rabbi Akiva:

“Akiva! Either way you will have to give an account.” In the Tosefta of Nedarim, chapter 5, Rabbi Yishmael said to him, “You have won it.” In [Eruvin 73a:5-8](https://www.sefaria.org/Eruvin.73a.5-8) he disagrees with Rabbi Yehudah ben Bava; in [Avodah Zarah 59b:4](https://www.sefaria.org/Avodah_Zarah.59b.4) both permit [wine] of an Israelite that a gentile poured as a libation not in the presence of an idol; in [Beitzah 29b:2](https://www.sefaria.org/Beitzah.29b.2): “In the name of Rabbi Papias and Rabbi Yehudah ben Beteira they said: One may sift a second time.” In Tosefta Gittin, chapter 2, Rabbi Yehudah ben Petirah disagrees

with Rabbi Yose HaGelili (and he is Rabbi Yehudah ben Beteira; the peh and bet interchange). In [Kiddushin 10b](https://www.sefaria.org/Kiddushin.10b.4-10), also cited in Sifrei Korach, on the verse “every pure one”: “[Rabbi] Yochanan ben Bag Bag sent to Rabbi Yehudah ben Beteira in Nisibis: I have heard of you that you say a betrothed Israelite woman eats terumah. He sent to him: And do you not say so? I hold you to be expert in the chambers of the Torah,

do you not know how to expound by a fortiori reasoning? … But what can I do, for the sages said: A betrothed Israelite woman does not eat terumah until she enters the wedding canopy.” Hyman continues: Now Rabbi Zacharias Frankel, author of Darkhei HaMishnah, comes, in that valuable book, p. 96, note 4, and raises a great difficulty: Is this not the enactment of the later Mishnah, after Rabbi Tarfon and Rabbi Akiva, as in the Mishnah cited at [Ketubot 57a:13](https://www.sefaria.org/Ketubot.57a.13), and Rabbi Yehudah ben Beteira lived a long time before this enactment?

Hyman replies: In fact it is no difficulty at all, for the first Mishnah and also the court after them, mentioned in the Mishnah, were a long time before Rabbi Tarfon, Rabbi Akiva and Rabbi Yehudah ben Beteira; and the dispute of Rabbi Tarfon and Rabbi Akiva, who disagreed in explaining the first Mishnah, concerns where there is no concern for a defect that could invalidate the marriage nor for “perhaps she will pour [terumah wine] for them,” and then the law of the first Mishnah stands in its place, and then their dispute applies also now. This is clear.

Hyman counts Rabbi Yehudah ben Beteira in the Mishnah fifteen times: Peah 3:7, Bikkurim 1:7, Shabbat 9:7, Pesachim 3:3, Yevamot 4:9, Ketubot 7:1, Nedarim 10:8, Gittin 2:4, Eduyot 8:3, Arakhin 8:4, Negaim 9:3 and 11:7, Kelim 2:4, Mikvaot 4:7; and in Shevuot 3:7 they said that by law he should be

liable, according to the words of Rabbi Yehudah ben Beteira. Likewise we find in the Mishnah “Ben Beteira” without further designation, as in Shabbat 4:3 and 15:1 and 15:3, Gittin 4:7, Zevachim 11:3 and Menachot 1:2; and so the Rambam holds in his Introduction to Zera’im, chapter 7, that Ben Beteira without further designation is Rabbi Yehoshua ben Beteira, and his intent is as they said in [Taanit 3a:11-12](https://www.sefaria.org/Taanit.3a.11-12): “Sometimes they call him by his own name (Rabbi Yehoshua ben

Beteira) and sometimes by his father’s name, and this was before they ordained him,” etc.; and Hyman cites Halikhot Olam (סק״פו) for the view that Ben Beteira without further designation is Rabbi Yehudah, and in Taanit there Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak answers under pressure. End of quotation. He is likewise mentioned in baraitot, as in [Bava Metzia 58b:5](https://www.sefaria.org/Bava_Metzia.58b.5), [Bava Batra 90b:10](https://www.sefaria.org/Bava_Batra.90b.10) and [Yevamot 121a:21](https://www.sefaria.org/Yevamot.121a.21).[^11] His great academy in Nisibis grew so much that the sages of the Land of Israel sought to go

to study before him, as in Sifrei Re’eh, on “When [the Lord] shall cut off”: an incident with Rabbi Elazar ben Shamua and Rabbi Yochanan HaSandlar, who were going to Nisibis to Rabbi Yehudah ben Beteira to study Torah from him; they reached Sidon and remembered the Land of Israel … and returned. And they said there: an incident with Rabbi Yehudah ben Beteira, Rabbi Matya ben Charash, Rabbi Chananyah, the nephew of Rabbi Yehoshua, and Rabbi Yonatan, who were going out abroad; they reached Paltom and remembered the Land of Israel … and rent

their garments … and returned and came to their place. The Yalkut there reads Rabbi Yehoshua instead of Rabbi Yonatan. Hyman finds the Sifrei very hard to understand, for as is known, apart from Rabbi Yonatan, all of them were most of their days abroad. Of his students only a few names remain to us. Rabbi Yoshiyah was his student, as in Jerusalem Talmud Sanhedrin 8:6, also cited in Sifrei Ki Tetze, section 31, where Rabbi Yoshiyah said: “When I came and presented the matters before

Rabbi Yehudah ben Beteira” (and in [Sotah 25a:16-17](https://www.sefaria.org/Sotah.25a.16-17) it reads: “And when I came to my colleagues in the South”). Elazar ben Pinchas cites Rabbi Yehudah ben Beteira in [Yoma 18a](https://www.sefaria.org/Yoma.18a.16), as in the printed Hyman text. A parallel appears in the [Tosefta Zavim](https://www.sefaria.org/Tosefta_Zavim.2.3) (chapter 1 in Hyman’s citation).[^9] Hyman observes that the names of his Babylonian students have not been preserved, just as the names of all the Babylonian sages of the early generations have not been preserved. Rabbi Yehudah ben Beteira lived long, for at the end

of Rabbi Akiva’s days we find in [Yevamot 108b:12](https://www.sefaria.org/Yevamot.108b.12) that they asked Rabbi Akiva in prison and he forbade it, [and asked] Rabbi Yehudah ben Beteira in Nisibis and he forbade it. And he lived also many years afterward, as in Jerusalem Talmud Sanhedrin 1:2 and Nedarim 6:8: when the sages of the generation after Rabbi Akiva — Rabbi Meir, Rabbi Yehudah and their other colleagues — gathered and sent a letter to Chananyah, the nephew of Rabbi Yehoshua, that he should no longer intercalate years, he went to consult with the elder

of the generation, Rabbi Yehudah ben Beteira, whether to listen to them; and on his advice Chananyah himself rode in order to reach the places where Israel lived and annul the calculation of his intercalation. Hyman concludes that by the days of Rabbi Yose or Rabbi Shimon he was already no longer alive, as we find in [Yevamot 102a:8-9](https://www.sefaria.org/Yevamot.102a.8-9): “Rabbi Yose said (in the Tosefta there it reads Rabbi Shimon said, but in Zuckermandel’s Tosefta it reads Rabbi Yose): Once I went to Nisibis

and found an elder. I said to him: Are you familiar with Rabbi Yehudah ben Beteira? He said to me: Yes, and I was regularly at his table,” etc. Hyman concludes: From this we see that he had already died then, and the elder told him an incident that had already happened. Therefore it is in no way possible to say that this Rabbi Yehudah ben Beteira lived long and was also in Rabbi’s days, as we will explain.

notes.text: Root read the complete supplied Hebrew, all 20 current/proposed English units and all current/historical substantive notes. Both heading spellings בתירא—בתירה are retained. Hyman owns the family descent, long-life reconstruction and chronological arguments, including his strong no-possibility conclusion; no genealogy is admitted. Supplied Peah3:7/Bikkurim1:7/Mikvaot4:7 remain in the body; saved ToratEmet357 passages match at3:6/1:6/4:5 respectively. Other supplied Mishnah locators remain literal, without old misleading question-mark substitutions. The Pesachim3:3 disagreement is one clause. Saved Davidson AZ59b makes the relevant object an idol, not an idolater. The Kiddushin10b question asks whether the addressee knows how to derive a kal vachomer; the quotation’s question boundary is restored. Supplemental Davidson Beitzah29b paragraph1 confirms שונין means sifting a second time, not merely sifting. ר״פ remains visible as the designated author of DarkheiHaMishnah; reviewer Frankel expansion has not been adopted without an independently read author witness. כל״ם is kept visibly in Hyman’s statement about receipt from his father; the model’s silent בל״ס/undoubtedly emendation is not established. סק״פו is retained without choosing186 versus subsection86; קבא is retained with saved Davidson Yevamot121a as a matching comparison, not page-history proof. Source ובתוספה כה. remains visible: the cited colleagues-in-the-South words occur in saved Davidson Sotah25a, and supplemental paragraphs15–16 explicitly name Yoshiyah, but Tosefta pagination is not categorically impossible and this does not prove an OCR correction. Eliezer follows supplied אליעזר בן פנחס, not draft Elazar; supplied זכים is disclosed as the proposed Zavim reading. These three units remain held for unresolved supplied abbreviations/bibliographic readings. Old source questions, variant readings and author conjectures remain preserved. Digital editions are not printed pixels or correction-history proof.

The supplied כל״ם has not been resolved here. The replacement English therefore supplies neither “all” nor “undoubtedly” as its meaning; “[his Torah]” is only the contextual object of receiving from his father, not a restored source word.

The supplied Mishnah references are retained. The consulted Torat Emet text of Eduyot 8:3 names Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel as the speaker accepting the testimony. Shevuot 3:6 contains the liability argument cited here as 3:7, and Arakhin 8:6 names Rabbi Yehudah ben Beteira alongside the supplied 8:4. The consulted Ketubot 7:1 names Rabbi Yehudah without the patronymic, and the cited Nedarim 10:8 has no named Beteira in that witness. The count of fifteen is Hyman’s. The Vilna edition of Rambam’s Introduction identifies the bare Ben Beteira as Rabbi Yehoshua ben Beteira. Taanit 3a discusses that identification for a particular baraita. The Halikhot Olam locator סק״פו remains unresolved. Menachot 1:2 has the bare name Ben Beteira. The consulted Shabbat 15:1 and 15:3, Gittin 4:7, and Zevachim 11:3 do not show that designation at those locators. The digital Shabbat 4:3 request did not resolve.

The consulted Tosefta Gittin gives Beteira where the supplied notice gives Petirah. Sifrei Bamidbar 117 gives the Ben Bag Bag exchange with “R. Yehudah” at Nisibis, while Kiddushin 10b gives the full name. The National Library of Israel catalogue lists Zacharias Frankel as the author of Darkhei HaMishnah. Hyman’s abbreviation ר״פ is retained, and the cited page and note have yet to be checked. The consulted Yalkut Shimoni 885 includes both Yehoshua and Yonatan, where Hyman reports a substitution. The place name appears as פלטוס there and פלטנום in the consulted Sifrei Devarim 80. Yoma 18a gives Elazar ben Pinchas, while the supplied notice gives Eliezer. The transmission was not located in the consulted Machon Mamre text of Tosefta Zavim chapter 1.

The Jerusalem Talmud parallels describe the letters sent by Rabbi through Yitzchak and Natan, Beteira’s advice at Nisibis, and Chananyah’s ride. Hyman’s placement of the episode and his chronology are his reconstruction. In the consulted Yevamot 102a, Rabbi Yose tells the story, and the elder says Beteira is a regular at the elder’s table. The consulted Tosefta Yevamot 12:8 gives the bracketed name Shimon and puts the elder’s statement in the past tense. Hyman’s quotation puts the elder at Beteira’s table. His report of the Zuckermandel reading remains uncollated.

The supplied Hebrew reads כל״ם. The inspected print (Hyman, vol. II, p. 556) reads בל״ס, “undoubtedly.” The English follows that printed reading. The inference about learning from his father in Nisibis is Hyman’s.

The printed Hyman p. 556 reads רז״פ where the supplied text has ר״פ. Zacharias Frankel’s Darkhei HaMishnah, p. 96, note 4, as recovered in public OCR, raises the chronology difficulty about the later Mishnah and refers to Tosafot Kiddushin 11a. The note is legible in that OCR comparison, and its original print has yet to be collated. Kiddushin 10b gives the question and the restriction, and the later court’s formulation spans Ketubot 57a–57b. Frankel’s difficulty and Hyman’s reply are their historical readings.

Hyman p. 557 gives Yevamot קכא. beside supplied קבא. The baraita begins at Yevamot 121a and the ruling continues at 121b. The printed Halikhot Olam locator is סק״פו. Its exact section remains uncertain. Taanit 3a’s discussion of the named and unnamed forms concerns the particular teaching under discussion.

Hyman p. 557 reads Sotah 25a, אלעזר בן פנחס, and Tosefta Zavim chapter 1, beside supplied תוספה, אליעזר and זכים. The named Sotah text has Yoshiyah’s report about his colleagues in the South. Yoma 18a gives Elazar ben Pinchas speaking in Yehudah ben Beteira’s name. A parallel in the consulted Tosefta is at Zavim 2:3, where the Hebrew uses the abbreviated ר״א בן פינחס and the Community Translation expands the name as Eliezer ben Pinchas. Hyman’s chapter 1 stays visible.

The story of Yehu’s trough appears at [Mikvaot 4:5](https://www.sefaria.org/Mishnah_Mikvaot.4.5) in the edition linked here. The same locator is listed in [Seder HaDorot 1619](https://www.girsology.com/seder-hadorot.html?entry=1619&lang=en). Heilprin also records competing accounts of how Rabbi Yehudah fits into the Beteira family. [Rosh Hashanah 29b:12–13](https://www.sefaria.org/Rosh_Hashanah.29b.12-13) names the Benei Beteira collectively. Hyman proposes a line of descent to explain the connection.

The later court’s statement begins at [Ketubot 57a:13](https://www.sefaria.org/Ketubot.57a.13) and continues at [Ketubot 57b:1](https://www.sefaria.org/Ketubot.57b.1), which gives entry under the wedding canopy as the condition. The baraita about the pit of snakes and scorpions likewise spans [Yevamot 121a:21](https://www.sefaria.org/Yevamot.121a.21) and [Yevamot 121b:1](https://www.sefaria.org/Yevamot.121b.1). There Rabbi Yehudah ben Beteira’s position is explained by the possibility that the person could charm the snakes.
